intro: Read the deck for the evidence and these notes for how to use it. Each note beside a slide explains how to read it, what to remember and where practitioners slip. Work the section examples with a pencil, answer the recall questions, and then run the activity profile on a programme you know.

sections.title: Sex, gender and why development cares
sections.big_idea: Sex is biology and gender is the **roles, rules and power** a society attaches to it, and the same programme lands differently on women and men.
in_plain_words: Sex refers to biological characteristics and explains why maternal health needs its own services. Gender refers to roles, rules, expectations and power, which are learned and change over time. Gender relations are the power relations between women and men and among each. A practitioner asks which differences need specific services and which can be changed.

A programme distributes money, land or training, and gender decides who receives it, who controls it, who does the extra work and who is consulted. Gender operates at four levels: individual, household, community and market, and state. Equality means equal rights and equity adjusts for different starting points. **Gender analysis studies relations, so it includes men.**

diagram.caption: change at one level can be blocked at another

key_terms.meaning: Biological characteristics: chromosomes, hormones, reproductive anatomy.
Roles, rules, expectations and power attached to being a woman or man.
Socially constructed power relations between and among women and men.
Measures that allow for different starting points.
Allows special provision for women and children.

worked_example.title: Read an NFHS-5 gap
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's NFHS-5 figures for women and men aged 15-49: literacy 72% against 84%, currently employed 25% against 75%.
steps: Literacy gap: 84 − 72 = 12 points.
Employment gap: 75 − 25 = 50 points.
The employment gap is larger by 50 − 12 = 38 points.
Place each at its level: literacy is shaped by individual and household decisions, employment by household, market and state.
worked_example.answer: A 12-point literacy gap and a 50-point employment gap, so schooling has outrun paid work.

mistakes: Treating all differences between women and men as biological.
Measuring only litres delivered or members enrolled and missing who gained time or income.
Counting women as a separate group and ignoring relations with men.
Assuming equal treatment of unequal people closes a gap.

recall.q: What is the difference between sex and gender?
recall.a: Sex refers to biological characteristics. Gender refers to the roles, rules, expectations and power a society attaches to being a woman or man.

recall.q: What are the four levels where gender operates?
recall.a: Individual, household, community and market, and state.

recall.q: Which Articles of the Constitution guarantee equality and allow special provision for women?
recall.a: Article 14 equality before the law, Article 15(1) no discrimination on sex, Article 15(3) special provision for women and children.

recall.q: Why does NFHS suit gender analysis?
recall.a: It asks the same questions of women and men and repeats them in each round.

sections.title: From WID to GAD: the ideas
sections.big_idea: Frameworks moved from adding women to **analysing power**, and Moser and Kabeer turned that into planning and measurement tools.
in_plain_words: Boserup showed that women did much farm work and that modernisation bypassed them. WID then argued women should be integrated into programmes, WAD located the problem in the world economy, and GAD made gender relations and power the object of analysis. DAWN added a Southern view that judged development by its effect on poor women.

Moser separated practical from strategic needs and described a triple role of reproductive, productive and community work. Kabeer defined empowerment through resources, agency and achievements. **Name which of the three dimensions an indicator measures** and what it leaves out, because a resource without agency overstates change.

events.what: Boserup's Woman's Role in Economic Development
WAD: the system is the problem
Moser on practical and strategic needs

diagram.caption: how the ideas built on each other

key_terms.meaning: Women in Development: integrate women into existing programmes.
Gender and Development: analyses relations and power.
Needs from existing roles, such as water near home.
Needs that change subordination, such as land rights.
The ability to define goals and act on them.

worked_example.title: Resource or agency?
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's NFHS table: a woman has a bank account she uses (resource) and takes part in three household decisions (agency). Bank account use rose from 53% in NFHS-4 to 79% in NFHS-5, and 89% in NFHS-6.
steps: Rise in account use to NFHS-5: 79 − 53 = 26 points.
Further rise to NFHS-6: 89 − 79 = 10 points.
Decision-making is 88.7% in NFHS-5 and 89% in NFHS-6, so it barely moved.
Kabeer's reading: resources moved far faster than agency, so reporting success on accounts alone overstates change.
worked_example.answer: Accounts rose 26 and then 10 points while decisions hardly changed, so check agency before claiming success.

mistakes: Using WID's 'add women and stir' as if it changed control over income.
Reading WAD as a theory of inequality within the household.
Meeting practical needs without asking whether a strategic gain is possible.
Taking an indicator out of context. The same act can mean different things in different places.

recall.q: What were Moser's three roles?
recall.a: Reproductive, productive and community managing.

recall.q: What is the difference between practical and strategic needs?
recall.a: Practical needs arise from existing roles and do not challenge them. Strategic needs arise from subordinate position and, if met, change it.

recall.q: What are Kabeer's three dimensions?
recall.a: Resources, agency and achievements.

recall.q: What did GAD lead to in 1995?
recall.a: Gender mainstreaming, adopted in the Beijing Platform for Action.

sections.title: Inside the household: bargaining and land
sections.big_idea: Households bargain, and **who holds income and assets** shapes what the household spends.
in_plain_words: The unitary model treats the household as one decision-maker with pooled income, so who receives a transfer would not matter. Bargaining models predict that spending depends on who controls the income. Sen described cooperative conflicts, with breakdown position, perceived interest and perceived contribution. Agarwal added norms, bargaining beyond the home and the strengthening effect of land, work, kin and collectives.

Land matters most in rural South Asia. The 2005 amendment made daughters coparceners by birth, and the Supreme Court in Vineeta Sharma (2020) removed the dependence on the father's date of death. Ownership, recognition and control can each be missing. **Who is named on the benefit is the cheapest gender decision a programme makes.**

left.title: Unitary model
items: Who receives a transfer does not matter
Policy can ignore who holds assets

right.title: Bargaining models
items: Spending depends on who controls income

key_terms.meaning: Household treated as one unit with pooled income.
How well off each person would be if cooperation ended.
A member with rights in joint family property by birth.
Assets and options a person has outside the household.
Assigning the recipient at random to test who decides.

worked_example.title: Size the ownership gaps
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's NFHS-5 figures for women and men aged 15-49 who own alone or jointly: land 32% against 42%, a house 42% against 60%.
steps: Land gap: 42 − 32 = 10 points.
House gap: 60 − 42 = 18 points.
Ownership is a resource. Check control separately: who decides on sale or mortgage?
Design: put the asset in a woman's name or in joint names, and record who decides.
worked_example.answer: Ten points on land and 18 on a house. Ownership is not the same as control, so measure both.

mistakes: Assuming household pooling, so the account goes to whoever is the head.
Counting nominal ownership as control when a male relative decides in practice.
Forgetting that Muslim, Christian and Parsi women inherit under different personal laws.
Supporting women individually when a collective would raise every member's fall-back position.

recall.q: What does the unitary model predict about transfers?
recall.a: That it makes no difference who in the household receives them.

recall.q: What are Sen's three factors in cooperative conflicts?
recall.a: Breakdown position, perceived interest and perceived contribution.

recall.q: What did Vineeta Sharma v Rakesh Sharma (2020) hold?
recall.a: That a daughter's coparcenary right arises by birth and does not depend on her father being alive on 9 September 2005.

recall.q: Name one risk of putting income in a woman's hands.
recall.a: Backlash or violence when her income or say rises.

sections.title: Missing women, son preference and sex ratios
sections.big_idea: Three sex ratios measure different things, and the **sex ratio at birth** isolates sex selection.
in_plain_words: Sen estimated that a great many more than 100 million women were missing by comparing actual numbers with a benchmark ratio. The overall sex ratio mixes births, deaths and migration. The child sex ratio reflects selection and excess mortality, and the sex ratio at birth isolates selection. The child sex ratio fell for fifty years even while the overall ratio rose.

Surveys show open son preference, and the imbalance comes from the minority with a strong preference and from demand for at least one son as fertility falls. The PCPNDT Act bans sex determination, BBBP launched in 2015, and neither isolates a single cause of improvement. **Target the demand for sons and protect access to safe reproductive care.**

diagram.caption: never quote one as if it were another

key_terms.meaning: Females per 1,000 males, all ages.
Girls per 1,000 boys aged 0-6.
Girls born per 1,000 boys born.
1994 Act banning sex determination and selection.
Daughters leave at marriage and sons stay to support parents.

worked_example.title: Convert boys per girl to girls per 1,000 boys
worked_example.setup: The deck converts the UN series from boys born per girl to girls per 1,000 boys. India 2024 is 1.071 and Sri Lanka 1.044.
steps: India: 1,000 ÷ 1.071 = 933.7, which the deck gives as 934.
Sri Lanka: 1,000 ÷ 1.044 = 957.9, which the deck gives as 958.
Difference between the two: 958 − 934 = 24.
For India itself, quote the SRS figure of 913 for 2021, since the UN series is modelled.
worked_example.answer: India 934 and Sri Lanka 958 in the UN series, a gap of 24. Use SRS for India.

mistakes: Mixing the census child sex ratio with the SRS sex ratio at birth.
Celebrating one year's rise from a small sample.
Messaging that stigmatises abortion in general, which pushes women to unsafe providers.
Conflating the MTP Act with the PCPNDT Act in communication.

recall.q: What are the latest India values for the three ratios?
recall.a: Overall 943 (Census 2011), child 918 (Census 2011) and at birth 913 (SRS 2021).

recall.q: What did the rising overall ratio and falling child ratio show?
recall.a: That the problem had concentrated at birth.

recall.q: What percentage of women want at least one son in NFHS-5?
recall.a: 81%, against 79% who want at least one daughter.

recall.q: Why do HMIS and SRS ratios not prove BBBP worked?
recall.a: They do not separate the scheme's effect from falling fertility, education or enforcement.

sections.title: Women's work and how it is measured
sections.big_idea: A women's employment figure depends on **who is asked, over what period and which activities count**.
in_plain_words: PLFS counts usual status over 365 days and current weekly status over 7 days. Usual status with subsidiary work counts seasonal and part-time work that short windows miss. Female LFPR rose from 23.3% to 41.7% between 2017-18 and 2023-24, mostly among rural women, but the headline cannot tell new paid jobs from recorded family work.

Women's earnings are far below men's, especially in self-employment, and 44.4% of women outside the labour force cite child care or home-making. Opportunity changes decisions, as Jensen's study shows. In your own surveys, ask women directly and activity by activity. **Never mix national survey and modelled series in one chart.**

diagram.caption: five questions before you quote the number

key_terms.meaning: Share of the population working, seeking or available for work.
Principal plus subsidiary activity over 365 days.
Activity in the last 7 days.
Another person answering for the woman.
A harmonised series that fills gaps with models.

worked_example.title: Read the PLFS rise and pay gap
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's PLFS figures: rural female LFPR 24.6% to 47.6%, all-India 23.3% to 41.7%; 2025 regular monthly pay Rs 24,217 for men and Rs 18,353 for women.
steps: Rural rise: 47.6 − 24.6 = 23.0 points.
All-India rise: 41.7 − 23.3 = 18.4 points.
Rural rise is larger by 23.0 − 18.4 = 4.6 points, so rural women drive the rise.
Women's pay as a share of men's: 18,353 ÷ 24,217 = 0.758, which the deck rounds to 76%.
worked_example.answer: A 23.0-point rural rise against 18.4 overall, and women earn about 76% of men's regular wages.

mistakes: Treating a rising LFPR as proof of better jobs when it may reflect women recorded as family workers.
Using a single question like 'Do you work?', which misses unpaid family work.
Comparing the 2025 calendar-year figure directly with July-June years.
Comparing monthly self-employed earnings without noting that hours differ.

recall.q: What does usual status (ps+ss) add that current weekly status misses?
recall.a: Subsidiary work of 30 days or more, which counts seasonal and part-time work.

recall.q: Which women drove the rise in LFPR?
recall.a: Rural women, from 24.6% to 47.6% against urban 20.4% to 28.0%.

recall.q: What is the largest pay gap in PLFS 2025?
recall.a: Self-employment, where women earn 36% of men's monthly pay.

recall.q: Which source should be used for India and which for comparison across countries?
recall.a: PLFS for India and the modelled ILO series only for cross-country comparison.

sections.title: Unpaid care and time use
sections.big_idea: Women do most unpaid work, so **time is a resource** and every programme must say whose time it uses.
in_plain_words: The Time Use Survey records what each person aged 6 and above did in each 30-minute slot for the previous 24 hours. In 2024, 81.5% of women did unpaid domestic work on the reference day against 27.1% of men, and women spend far more of the day on it. Between 2019 and 2024 the shift was small: 315 to 305 minutes.

Time poverty and the double burden mean paid work added without unpaid work removed raises total hours. Elson's 3R framework gives the response. Design programmes around women's time with meetings at times women choose, creches and fuel and water investments, and add a short time-use module to baseline and endline. **Say what the programme adds to women's total work.**

key_terms.meaning: NSO survey recording 24 hours in 30-minute slots.
Too little time left after paid and unpaid work.
Paid work added with no cut in unpaid work.
Recognise, reduce, redistribute unpaid care.
Programme timing and tasks set around women's hours.

worked_example.title: Turn a share of the day into hours
worked_example.setup: The deck gives the share of the whole day that women and men aged 6+ spend on unpaid domestic work: 16.4% against 1.7%. A day has 24 hours.
steps: Women: 24 × 0.164 = 3.94 hours.
Gap: 3.94 − 0.41 = 3.53 hours a day, consistent with the deck's 'more than three hours'.
Change since 2019 for women who do the work: 315 − 305 = 10 minutes.
worked_example.answer: About 3.5 hours a day separates women and men, and the 2019 to 2024 change is only 10 minutes.

mistakes: Counting attendance at a meeting while ignoring the unpaid work it displaces.
Training for five full days away from home with no child care.
Judging infrastructure by cost per unit alone and missing hours saved for women and girls.
Quoting another country's minutes without checking its age group and reference day.

recall.q: How long is the recall period in the Time Use Survey and how is it divided?
recall.a: 24 hours, recorded in 30-minute slots.

recall.q: What share of women and men did unpaid caregiving on the reference day?
recall.a: 34.0% of women against 17.9% of men.

recall.q: What does the double burden mean?
recall.a: Women take up paid work with no matching cut in unpaid work, so total hours rise.

recall.q: What is a cheap way to see whether a programme added to women's work?
recall.a: A short time-use module (a 24-hour recall) at baseline and endline.

sections.title: Education and health gaps
sections.big_idea: Girls have gained in schooling, but gaps in health, phones and work remain, and **most barriers are social**.
in_plain_words: Literacy is 72% for women and 84% for men in NFHS-5, and the gap is widest among older women and in poorer and rural households. Girls leave school because of distance, domestic work, marriage, sanitation and low returns. Child marriage before 18 fell from 23% to 20.1% for women aged 20 to 24.

Anaemia affects 57% of women against 25% of men, girls are taken to providers later, and adult women need permission to travel. Norms also harm men, with 39% using tobacco against 4% of women. Phones matter too, since messages to the household number reach the man. **Always disaggregate health service data by sex and age.**

diagram.note: use the same indicator, same source, adjacent columns

key_terms.meaning: Women and men side by side for the same indicator and source.
Low haemoglobin; 57% of women aged 15-49 in NFHS-5.
Gender gap in phones and internet use.
Whether and when a person gets health care.
Reporting by sex and age.

worked_example.title: Build a gap table
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's NFHS-5 figures for ages 15-49: schooling of 10 or more years 41% women and 50% men, internet use 33% and 51%, anaemia 57% and 25%.
steps: Schooling gap: 50 − 41 = 9 points.
Internet gap: 51 − 33 = 18 points.
Anaemia gap: 57 − 25 = 32 points.
In NFHS-6, internet use is 64.3% for women and 80.5% for men, a gap of 80.5 − 64.3 = 16.2 points, so the gap narrowed.
worked_example.answer: Gaps of 9, 18 and 32 points in NFHS-5, with the internet gap narrowing to about 16 points in NFHS-6.

mistakes: Mixing NFHS-5 and NFHS-6 in one comparison without saying so. NFHS-6 does not report literacy or anaemia.
Assuming parity in college enrolment means parity in employment.
Sending messages to 'the household number' and assuming they reach women.
Treating women's anaemia as purely biological.

recall.q: Name three reasons girls leave school.
recall.a: Any three of: distance and safety, domestic work, marriage, sanitation, low returns to education.

recall.q: What percentage of women aged 20 to 24 were married before 18 in NFHS-6?
recall.a: 20.1%, down from 23% in NFHS-5.

recall.q: What is the maternal mortality figure for 2019-21?
recall.a: 93 per 1,00,000 live births, down from 130 in 2014-16.

recall.q: Why include men's health in gender analysis?
recall.a: Norms of toughness harm men's health and enlisting men helps change norms that hurt women.

sections.title: Violence against women: data and law
sections.big_idea: Violence is common and help-seeking is rare, so programmes need a **referral map before the first disclosure**.
in_plain_words: NFHS-5 reports that 32% of ever-married women aged 18 to 49 experienced spousal violence, and these are lower bounds. Only 14% of women who experienced physical or sexual violence sought help, and among them 61% turned to family and 6% to the police. Norms that justify violence are shared by women and men.

The law includes the PWDVA 2005 with a right to reside in the shared household, the BNS replacing the IPC from 1 July 2024, and the POSH Act 2013 with Internal and Local Committees. Enforcement gaps remain. When someone discloses violence, listen, check safety, refer, record minimally and follow up only if safe. **Never mediate between a woman and her abuser.**

diagram.caption: what a programme does when violence is disclosed

key_terms.meaning: Civil remedy law with protection, residence and monetary orders.
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, replacing the IPC from 1 July 2024.
2013 law on sexual harassment of women at work.
Employer committee presided over by a senior woman.
District body for small workplaces or complaints against employers.

worked_example.title: Who gets help?
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: of every 1,000 women who experienced physical or sexual violence, use the NFHS-5 shares in the deck: 14% sought help, 61% of those turned to family and 6% to the police.
steps: Women seeking help: 1,000 × 0.14 = 140.
Turning to family: 140 × 0.61 = 85.4.
Turning to the police: 140 × 0.06 = 8.4.
So 860 of every 1,000 did not seek help at all.
worked_example.answer: About 140 seek help, roughly 85 go to family and about 8 to the police.

mistakes: Treating a low reported rate as proof of low prevalence.
Publishing detailed case information that could identify a survivor.
Pushing a woman to report or mediating with the abuser.
Treating a staff POSH committee as covering programme participants. Safeguarding is a separate duty.

recall.q: What share of ever-married women 18-49 experienced spousal violence in NFHS-5?
Which PWDVA section gives the right to reside in the shared household?
recall.a: Section 17.

recall.q: How long does a woman have to complain under the POSH Act?
recall.a: Three months of the incident, extendable by three months.

recall.q: What are the five steps when violence is disclosed?
recall.a: Listen, safety, refer, record, follow up only if safe.

sections.title: Political representation
sections.big_idea: Reserved seats change policy, but **implementation of the 2023 reservation depends on census and delimitation**.
in_plain_words: The 73rd and 74th Amendments reserve at least one-third of panchayat and municipal seats for women, and many states raised panchayat reservation to 50%. Because reservation was assigned close to random, studies show women leaders invest in goods women ask for and change aspirations, and reports of crimes rise partly through greater reporting. Proxy rule persists.

The Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam reserves about one-third of Lok Sabha and Assembly seats, effective only after a delimitation based on the first census after commencement. It does not cover the Rajya Sabha or Legislative Councils. **Know the text and the current status** before joining the debate.

events.what: Act notified in force; seats not yet reserved
131st Amendment Bill defeated in Lok Sabha
Census reference date with caste enumeration

key_terms.meaning: Reserves panchayat seats and chair offices for women and SC/ST.
A husband or male relative running the elected woman's office.
Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam inserting Articles 330A and 332A.
Makes reservation effective after delimitation.
Reserved seats move between constituencies.

worked_example.title: Check the vote and the seats
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's figures: 528 members present and voting, a two-thirds majority needed, 298 votes in favour. India elected 78 women to the Lok Sabha in 2019 and 74 in 2024.
steps: Two-thirds of 528: 528 × 2 ÷ 3 = 352 votes needed.
Shortfall: 352 − 298 = 54 votes.
Change in women elected: 78 − 74 = 4 fewer in 2024.
The Bill needed a two-thirds majority of those present and voting because it amended the Constitution under Article 368.
worked_example.answer: 352 votes were needed, so the Bill fell 54 votes short. Women elected fell by 4 to 74.

mistakes: Saying the 2023 reservation is already in effect. It waits on census and delimitation.
Assuming proxy cases mean reservation changed nothing. Reserved seats still change policy on average.
Claiming an OBC sub-quota exists in the constitutional text.
Comparing parliament shares across countries without checking each year.

recall.q: What does Article 243D(3) reserve?
recall.a: Not less than one-third of directly elected panchayat seats for women, including SC and ST women.

recall.q: Why is the evidence from reservation unusually credible?
recall.a: Reservation was assigned by rotation that was close to random.

recall.q: Which houses does the 2023 reservation not cover?
recall.a: The Rajya Sabha and state Legislative Councils.

recall.q: What is the proxy reduction advice in the deck?
recall.a: Train elected women, back them with collectives, require their own presence and signature, and hold Mahila Sabhas before Gram Sabhas.

sections.title: Masculinities and intersectionality
sections.big_idea: Men are gendered too, and gender combines with caste, class and religion to produce **specific disadvantage**.
in_plain_words: Connell argued that there are several masculinities, ranked, with a hegemonic form that shapes expectations. Provider, protector and lineage ideals are strained by unemployment and debt. Programmes work with men as clients, partners, agents of change or by questioning norms, each with a risk, and they should be accountable to women.

Crenshaw named intersectionality, and in South Asia the most consequential intersection is gender with caste. Chakravarti argues caste endogamy depends on controlling women. Spousal violence is higher among Scheduled Caste women than other women, and the gap between wealth quintiles is larger than the gap between religions. **Disaggregate by one more axis at a time** and plan sample sizes for subgroups.

diagram.caption: all four stay accountable to women

key_terms.meaning: The most honoured form of manhood in a place and time.
How social categories combine to shape disadvantage.
Chakravarti's term for caste control over women's sexuality.
Breaking data down by sex and another axis.
Choosing women at specific intersections to interview.

worked_example.title: Which gap is bigger?
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's NFHS-5 figures for ever-experienced spousal physical or sexual violence: Scheduled Caste women 34.7%, other women 22.6%, Hindu 29.9%, Muslim 27.5%, poorest quintile 38.4%, richest 16.9%.
steps: Caste gap: 34.7 − 22.6 = 12.1 points.
Religion gap: 29.9 − 27.5 = 2.4 points.
Wealth gap: 38.4 − 16.9 = 21.5 points.
Wealth gap is bigger than the religion gap by 21.5 − 2.4 = 19.1 points, so check region, wealth and education before attributing a gap to religion.

mistakes: Rewarding men for minimal change in attitudes.
Measuring a men's programme only by men's attitudes and not by what women report.
Attributing a violence gap to religion without checking wealth.
Over-interpreting a single cell in a cross-tabulation of a small group.

recall.q: What is intersectionality?
recall.a: The analysis of how social categories combine to produce specific forms of advantage and disadvantage.

recall.q: How should a programme with men report results?
recall.a: By what changed for women, measured by asking women.

recall.q: What are the four steps of intersectional analysis in the deck?
recall.a: Disaggregate, cross, control, and listen.

recall.q: What is the paradox noted about caste and women's work?
recall.a: In some upper-caste households women's paid work outside the home is restricted as a status marker, so higher caste can mean lower participation.

sections.title: Practical application: gender analysis
sections.big_idea: Choose a framework for your question, then run an **activity profile**, a checklist and indicators with women and men.
in_plain_words: The Harvard framework profiles who does what and who controls resources. Moser reviews roles and needs, the Social Relations Approach looks at institutions and power, and the Gender Analysis Matrix works with communities. The activity profile is filled in with women and men separately, and disagreements between the versions are findings.

A design checklist covers analysis and design, and indicators should cover resources, agency, achievements and norms, reported for women and men at baseline and endline. The Bihar goat example shows tools turning into design changes. **Meet a practical need in a way that builds strategic gains.**

diagram.caption: choose the tool that answers your question

key_terms.meaning: Who does which task and who controls the result.
Profiles activities, access and control.
Participatory review of changes for women, men, households.
Prompts for analysis and for design and monitoring.
The source that shows an indicator moved.

worked_example.title: Add up the hours in the Bihar goat plan
worked_example.setup: Illustrative, from the deck: an NGO trains 2,000 women in goat rearing, and grazing adds about two hours a day for each woman.
steps: Added hours across the programme: 2,000 × 2 = 4,000 hours a day.
Design change: stall-feeding and shared grazing rotations to reduce that load.
Bargaining risk: husbands may claim sale proceeds, so put goats in women's names and pay into women's accounts.
Risk plan: referral map, trained staff, POSH committee.
worked_example.answer: The programme would add about 4,000 hours of work a day without the design changes.

mistakes: Using one framework for every question.
Filling the activity profile in a mixed meeting where men speak for women.
Using the checklist without discussion with women in the programme area.
Reporting women's attendance as an outcome.

recall.q: Which framework suits institutional and power analysis?
recall.a: The Social Relations Approach.

recall.q: How should the activity and access profile be filled in?
recall.a: With women and men separately, then compared.

recall.q: Why use NFHS wording in your surveys?
recall.a: It lets you compare your programme area with the district or state figure.

recall.q: When should the design checklist be used?
recall.a: At design, at mid-term review and before scale-up.

sections.title: Bringing it together
sections.big_idea: Be accurate about what a programme does, from **gender-blind to relation-changing**, and avoid the six common mistakes.
in_plain_words: A programme can be gender-blind, gender-aware, gender-responsive or relation-changing. Most sit in the middle, and claiming transformation for a change of meeting times costs credibility. Ask which relation changed, for whom, and what evidence shows it.

The six common mistakes are counting women as the result, assuming pooling, ignoring time, treating women as one group, leaving out men and mixing data sources. The summary reminds you that women aged 6 and over who do unpaid domestic work spend 289 minutes a day on it (2024). **Gender analysis is a habit of asking who does, who has, who decides and who benefits.**

diagram.caption: four types of programme, with the deck's examples

key_terms.meaning: Ignores gender differences.
Recognises differences and adjusts delivery.
Meets women's specific needs.
Changes underlying relations and norms.
Assuming income is shared as one pot.

worked_example.title: Classify three programmes and convert minutes
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: three programmes are described, and the deck says women aged 6 and over who do unpaid domestic work spend 289 minutes a day on it (2024).
steps: Training is held at 11 am at the block office with no child care: gender-blind.
Separate sessions for women are added: gender-aware.
A creche is added at the worksite: gender-responsive.
Joint land titles plus community work on inheritance would be relation-changing, with evidence of which relation changed.
289 minutes is 289 ÷ 60 = 4.8 hours a day.
worked_example.answer: Blind, aware, responsive, and relation-changing for joint titles. The 289 minutes is about 4.8 hours.

mistakes: Claiming transformation for a programme that only adjusts timings.
Assuming household pooling and putting the benefit in the household head's name.
Mixing data sources in one comparison.
Leaving men out for fear of diluting focus.

recall.q: What are the four types of programme in the decision table?
recall.a: Gender-blind, gender-aware or sensitive, gender-responsive and relation-changing.

recall.q: What is the correction for 'counting women as the result'?
recall.a: Measure what changed in their resources and agency.

recall.q: What question should you ask of any claim of transformation?
recall.a: Which relation changed, for whom, and what evidence shows it.

recall.q: Which course does the deck suggest first?
recall.a: Gender Mainstreaming 101, then WEE or Care Economy depending on your work.

notes.2: Use the agenda to plan your route. Sections 2 and 3 give the ideas, 4 to 8 give the evidence, 9 and 10 cover power and identity, and 11 gives the working tools. If you design programmes, **go to section 11 first** and return to the earlier sections as reference.
notes.4: Hold the two questions the slide ends on: which differences are biological and need specific services, and which are social and can change? Pregnancy needs maternal health services. Who fetches the water **is learned and varies by place**. The gender relations definition is about power.
notes.5: Test every programme you know with four questions: who receives, who controls afterwards, who does the extra work, who is consulted? The dairy and water examples show the same input producing different outcomes. Whose name is on the title, **whose phone gets the message** and when the meeting is held all matter.
notes.6: Read these five numbers as the opening of sections 4 to 8. Women outnumber men in households at 1,020 per 1,000, yet girls are missing at birth (928 for ages 0 to 6). Literacy, employment and violence follow. The slide notes NFHS-6 does not report these five **in the same form**.
notes.7: Trace a programme through the four levels, individual, household, community and market, state. The scholarship example shows how change at one level can be blocked at another. If a result surprises you, **look for the level where the block sits**.
notes.8: Separate equality from equity. Equality is equal rights (Articles 14, 15(1), 39(d)). Equity adjusts for different starting points (Article 15(3)). Reservation, girls' scholarships and women-only self-help groups rest on equity. The slide's warning is balanced: **equal treatment of unequal people preserves the gap**.
notes.9: The table shows the shift from counting to relations. Counting asks how many women were trained. Analysis asks who released her time and who covered her work. For land, ask who decides on sale. **A programme that ignores men often meets their resistance later.**
notes.10: Use this slide as a map of the course's three blocks: concepts and evidence, law and politics, and practice. It also names three deeper courses for budgeting, livelihoods and care. Note the final line: **statistics carry their sources and facts are stated as of October 2026**.
notes.12: Remember Boserup's argument in two parts: women did much farm work, and modernisation often bypassed them. Planners treated the male farmer as the norm. The plough finding adds a long-run idea: **descendants of plough societies show lower female participation today**.
notes.13: Learn WID as 'add women and stir'. It made women visible and argued in efficiency terms, but it left the division of labour and power untouched. Notice the example of tailoring and pickle-making: such projects **added to women's work without changing control over income**.
notes.14: WAD asked why women are poor and answered with the structure of the world economy. The table sets it against WID. Its weakness is the point to remember: it **folded gender into class** and said little about a poor woman and a poor man in the same household.
notes.15: Compare WID and GAD row by row. GAD shifts focus from women to relations, from exclusion to unequal power, and from efficiency to equality and transformation. It led to gender mainstreaming at Beijing in 1995. **Women become agents of change as well as beneficiaries.**
notes.16: DAWN changed the starting question from 'what can development do for women' to 'what does this model of development do to poor women'. It linked debt and structural adjustment to women's unpaid work. The South Asian roots, from Chipko to self-employed women's unions, tied together **livelihoods, violence and political voice**.
notes.17: Sort every project you meet into practical or strategic needs. Water near the home is practical. Land rights and freedom from violence are strategic. Most projects meet the first. The designer's question is whether the way they are met **also opens a strategic gain**.
notes.18: Learn the three roles: reproductive, productive and community managing. Women carry all three at once. A project that adds a demand on women's time without removing another can succeed at the cost of rest and health. **Ask whose unpaid time the project assumes is free.**
notes.19: Remember Kabeer's chain of resources, agency and achievements. The bank account example is the lesson: **a resource is not agency**. If you measure only resources you overstate change. The caution matters too, because the same act means different things in different places.
notes.20: Use this table to see the three dimensions in survey form. Bank account use rose from 53 to 79 percent, but decision-making changed much less. That gap is exactly what Kabeer's framework asks you to check. **Name the dimension each indicator measures and what it leaves out.**
notes.21: Treat the table as a menu of questions. WID asks if women are included, WAD on what terms, GAD who holds power, Moser which needs, Kabeer whether she can choose. When a donor asks for 'gender analysis', **ask which question they want answered**.
notes.23: The unitary model predicts that who receives a transfer makes no difference. Bargaining models predict that it does. Random assignment of the recipient is the cleanest test. The design consequence is concrete: **whose name goes on the account, ration card, title or policy** is a decision, so record it.
notes.24: Sen's three factors explain why women often lose in household bargaining: weaker breakdown position, norms that put the family first, and unpaid work seen as less contribution. The practical insight is the last line: **visible, paid work can raise bargaining power before income does**.
notes.25: Agarwal adds that norms limit what can be bargained over, that bargaining happens with community, market and state too, and that land, work, kin and women's groups strengthen a position. A collective **raises every member's fall-back position at once**, which individual help cannot.
notes.26: Note why land matters more than wages: it gives food, collateral, a fall-back in widowhood and standing. Then separate ownership from control. A daughter may inherit on paper and give up her share. The two ownership comparisons, **32% against 42%** for land, show the gap.
notes.27: Know the two legal anchors: the 2005 amendment made daughters coparceners by birth, and Vineeta Sharma (2020) held that the right does not depend on the father being alive on 9 September 2005. Then read the second box. The law is only part of the story, since **mutation of records and family pressure** remain barriers.
notes.28: Match each method to the question it can answer and the blind spot it carries. Survey modules give reported say, expenditure comparisons test pooling, randomised transfers give causal effect, and interviews explain why. **Combine a survey measure with qualitative work** for the most informative design.
notes.29: Convert the left box into a design checklist and the right box into a list of risks to watch. The strongest line is the last one. Track both resources and agency, because **a joint title is a resource and the decision on sale is agency**.
notes.31: Follow Sen's method: compare actual women with the number expected at a benchmark ratio. The benchmark of 1.05 shows what equal care produces. Kerala's ratio above 1.03 shows the deficit is social. Remember the closing point that **growth alone does not close the gap**.
notes.32: Memorise the three ratios and their sources: overall 943, child 918, at birth 913. Each isolates something different. The sex ratio at birth isolates selection, because slightly more boys are born anywhere. Surveys give different values from the census because **they cover different populations**.
notes.33: Read the chart as a fifty-year decline after 1981, when ultrasound became cheap. The key reasoning is in the last two sentences. The overall ratio rose from 933 to 943 while the child ratio fell, so **the problem had concentrated at birth**.
notes.34: Notice that most families want both sexes, with 81 percent wanting at least one son and 79 percent at least one daughter. The imbalance comes from a minority with a strong preference and from the demand for at least one son as fertility falls. **Sex selection becomes the means when fertility is low.**
notes.35: Learn the Act in four parts: what is banned (section 6), clinic registration, the penalties, and the authorities. The closing paragraph is a candid assessment. **Convictions are few and a ban on technology does not change the demand** that drives sex selection.
notes.36: Read BBBP as a scheme launched in 2015 in 100 districts and extended to 640 in 2018. HMIS shows 918 rising to 937, and SRS 899 rising to 913. Both improve, but **neither isolates the scheme's effect** from falling fertility, education or enforcement. That needs an evaluation design.
notes.37: Use the table for cross-country comparison only. India stands out at 934 girls per 1,000 boys in the UN series. For India itself, quote SRS. The note explains why the two differ: **one is modelled from several sources and the other is a direct sample count**.
notes.38: Use the two columns as a communications check. Raise the value of daughters, work with mothers-in-law and husbands, and monitor district data. Avoid stigmatising abortion or celebrating one year's rise. The rule of thumb to remember: **target the demand for sons and protect access to safe care**.
notes.40: Check three things before reading any women's employment figure: age group, reference period and which activities count. Usual status looks back 365 days and counts subsidiary work of 30 days or more. Current weekly status looks at 7 days. **Short windows undercount women's intermittent work.**
notes.41: Note the rise in female LFPR from 23.3 to 41.7 percent between 2017-18 and 2023-24 while male LFPR barely moved. The last bar, 40.0 percent in 2025, is calendar-year data. It is **not strictly comparable with the July-June years**, so read the footnote.
notes.42: Rural women explain most of the rise: 24.6 to 47.6 percent against 20.4 to 28.0 in urban areas. The headline cannot tell new paid jobs from women in farm households being recorded as family workers. The cautious reading is the one to quote: **more women are being counted as working**.
notes.43: Read the third column as women's pay as a share of men's: 76, 36 and 69 percent. The self-employed gap is largest and most women workers are self-employed. Remember the caution that hours differ, so **monthly gaps overstate the gap per hour**.
notes.44: Contrast the two reasons: 44.4 percent of women outside the labour force cite child care or home-making, while 69.8 percent of men cite studies. That is the gender division of labour in one pair of numbers. **Supply and demand both matter**, so train women only where employers hire them.
notes.45: Never mix national survey and modelled series in one chart. The ILO estimate for India in 2025 is 32.4 percent against 40.0 in PLFS. Use PLFS for India and the modelled series only **for cross-country comparison**, as the slide states.
notes.46: Jensen's study shows that credible information about women's earning opportunities changes how families invest in girls. Recruitment services raised girls' enrolment and nutrition. The second paragraph adds a practical idea: **transport, lighting and safe workplaces are labour market policies for women**.
notes.47: Fix the five survey problems before fielding your own questionnaire. Ask women directly, ask activity by activity, use a 12-month recall as well as 7 days, and train interviewers. The warning at the end matters most for trend data: **every method change alters the rate**.
notes.49: Understand what time use adds to a labour survey. A labour survey counts people as working or not. The Time Use Survey records minutes in each 30-minute slot over 24 hours, including unpaid domestic and caregiving work that national accounts leave out. It enumerated **4,54,192 persons** in 2024.
notes.50: Read participation next to minutes. 81.5 percent of women did unpaid domestic work on the reference day against 27.1 percent of men, and 34.0 percent of women did unpaid caregiving against 17.9 percent of men. **Both the share doing the work and the minutes differ.**
notes.51: Treat 2019 to 2024 as small shifts. Women's minutes on unpaid domestic services fell from 315 to 305, and the share of women 15-59 in employment rose from 21.8 to 25 percent. Against a gap of more than three hours a day, **five years is a short period for norms**.
notes.52: Time poverty is too little time left for rest, learning and public life. The double burden is paid work added without unpaid work removed. Elson's 3R framework gives the way out: recognise, reduce, redistribute. **State whose time a programme uses and what it removes.**
notes.53: Use the table as a design review. For each row, check which version your programme resembles: meetings at the block office or in the village, five days away or short sessions with child care. A short 24-hour recall module shows **whether the programme added to women's total work**.
notes.54: Compare countries by the direction of the gap and leave exact minutes to within-country analysis, because definitions and reference days differ. India's gap of more than three hours a day is the benchmark. **Open each office's report** before quoting another country's figure.
notes.56: Use these figures to see gains and gaps. Literacy is 72 against 84 percent, schooling of 10 or more years is 46.4 against 54.6 in NFHS-6, and internet use is 64.3 against 80.5. In higher education women are ahead in numbers, but **college parity does not yet mean parity in employment**.
notes.57: Match each barrier to a response: distance and safety to bicycles and nearby schools, domestic work to creches, marriage to conditional transfers and enforcement, sanitation to toilets. Child marriage has the clearest legal answer and fell from 23 to 20.1 percent for women aged 20 to 24.
notes.58: Read the three health figures together: anaemia at 57 percent for women against 25 for men, maternal mortality at 93 per 1,00,000 in 2019-21, and thinness. The slide's summary line is the one to keep. **Women's health gaps are partly biological and largely social.**
notes.59: The slide splits care-seeking into girls and adult women. Girls are taken to providers later and less often. Adult women need permission or company, and three-fifths report at least one problem getting care. The programme advice is simple and cheap: **disaggregate health data by sex and age**.
notes.60: Gender analysis includes men. Norms of toughness link to tobacco and alcohol use and to late care-seeking. In NFHS-5, 39 percent of men use tobacco against 4 percent of women. Treating men's health needs also helps **enlist men as allies in changing norms** that hurt women.
notes.61: Check whose phone receives the message and whether she can read it. In NFHS-6, 63.6 percent of women have a phone they use, up from 54 percent, and 71 percent of women with a phone can read text messages. Programmes sending to 'the household number' **usually reach the man**.
notes.62: Use this as a model gender table: same indicator, same source, women and men side by side. The gaps run from 9 points in schooling to 50 in employment. The closing explanation links it all: **schooling has risen faster than paid work, and unpaid care absorbs the difference**.
notes.64: Treat 32 percent as a lower bound, since some women do not disclose. NFHS-6 reports 22.3 percent for physical or sexual violence against 29 in NFHS-5. Only 14 percent sought help, and 6 percent of those turned to the police. Physical violence at 28 percent is the most common form.
notes.65: The chart shows violence at every level of caste and wealth, higher for Scheduled Caste and poorer households. Caste and wealth overlap, so the chart cannot separate them. **Do not attribute a gap to one factor** without controlling for the other, as section 10 explains.
notes.66: The attitude figures are 45 percent of women and 44 percent of men agreeing with at least one reason for a husband to beat his wife. Women's agreement shows how widely a norm is shared, including by those it harms. Use NFHS wording so you can **compare with the state figure**.
notes.67: Know the PWDVA as a civil remedy alongside criminal law. The broad definition in section 3 includes economic abuse and dowry harassment. Section 17, the right to reside in the shared household, is **often the most valuable remedy** for a woman with nowhere else to go.
notes.68: Learn both numbering systems: cruelty 498A became BNS 85, dowry death 304B became 80, rape 375 became 63, from 1 July 2024. Old cases stay under old sections. The exception to s63 and the pending challenges are live, so **check the current status** before advising anyone.
notes.69: Trace the path from Vishaka (1997) to the POSH Act 2013. The table gives the working rules: Internal Committee, Local Committee for small workplaces, complaint within three months, inquiry within ninety days, fine up to Rs 50,000. **Know the deadlines** because they decide whether a complaint proceeds.
notes.70: The Supreme Court found serious lapses in Internal Committees in 2023 and has pushed for a dashboard. Use the right-hand box as an NGO checklist: constitute the committee, publish members, train them, cover field staff and report. **POSH covers staff and safeguarding covers participants**, which are separate duties.
notes.71: Use the table to compare South Asian laws, but read the last line for the real lesson. In some districts of Bangladesh a 2020 study found no cases filed in a decade. **A law nobody uses signals weak awareness, distant courts or fear at home.**
notes.72: Memorise the five-step response: listen, safety, refer, record, follow up. Build the referral map before the programme begins. Never mediate between a woman and her abuser or push her to report. Violence data are the **most harmful kind of personal data**, so collect only what is necessary.
notes.74: Remember Article 243D(3) and (4): one-third of seats and one-third of chairperson offices, with Article 243T for municipal seats. Many states raised it to 50 percent. Rotation spreads exposure but often **prevents re-election from a seat that becomes unreserved**.
notes.75: Match each study to its finding. Chattopadhyay and Duflo found investment in goods women ask for. Beaman and colleagues found narrower aspiration gaps and attitudes changing after a second round. Iyer and colleagues found more crime reports. **Near-random reservation makes the evidence unusually credible.**
notes.76: Proxy rule is real and so is the policy effect. Both are true at once. Look at what reduces proxies: training, collectives, a requirement for the elected member's own presence and signature, and Mahila Sabhas before Gram Sabhas. **Design support for the elected woman herself.**
notes.77: Compare women's share of parliament across South Asia in the chart, and note Nepal's constitutional one-third rule. India elected 74 women to the 18th Lok Sabha, 13.6 percent, down from 78 in 2019. **Check the year of each country's figure** before comparing.
notes.78: Read the text before the headlines. The 106th Amendment reserves about one-third of Lok Sabha and Assembly seats, including within SC and ST seats. Article 334A makes it effective after a delimitation based on the first census after commencement. It excludes the **Rajya Sabha and Legislative Councils**.
notes.79: Use the dates as a status table. The Act was notified into force on 16 April 2026, but seats are not yet reserved because Article 334A needs census and delimitation. The 131st Amendment Bill got 298 votes against 352 needed. **Watch the census publication date.**
notes.80: Present both sides fairly. The case for cites panchayat evidence and the share of women in the Lok Sabha. The concerns include delay and rotation. The text already includes SC and ST women, and has no OBC sub-quota because the Constitution has no OBC legislative reservation. **Know the text before you debate it.**
notes.81: Use the table to look beyond legislatures: Gram Sabha attendance, district posts, courts, unions and cooperatives, programme committees. For committees the test is simple. **A committee with women members that never meets is a paper reform**, so check who attends and influences decisions.
notes.83: Connell's point is that masculinities are plural and ranked, and the dominant form shapes expectations even for men who do not live up to it. Unemployment, migration and debt threaten the provider ideal. Working with men on these norms **is part of preventing violence**.
notes.84: Choose an approach and know its risk: men as clients can divert funds from women's services, partners can reinforce men as decision-makers, agents of change can reward minimal change, and norm-changing is slow. Keep accountability to women, and **ask women what changed**.
notes.85: Crenshaw's insight is that categories combine to produce experiences that single-category analysis misses. In South Asia the most consequential intersection is gender with caste. Dalit feminists made the argument earlier. For practitioners, the definition tells you to **look at categories together and never one at a time**.
notes.86: Read the table: spousal physical or sexual violence is 34.7 percent for Scheduled Caste women and 22.6 percent for other women. Chakravarti's argument is that caste endogamy depends on controlling women. The paradox at the end shows **higher caste can mean lower women's participation**.
notes.87: Use the table for the other identities, and pay attention to the closing example. The religion gap in violence (29.9 and 27.5) is smaller than the gap between the poorest and richest quintiles (38.4 and 16.9). **Check region, wealth and education before attributing a gap to religion.**
notes.88: Follow the four steps: disaggregate by sex and one other axis, cross them, control, and listen. Report confidence intervals for small groups and avoid over-reading a single cell. Hold focus groups separately **so dominant groups do not speak for others**.
notes.90: Choose the framework to match your question. Harvard profiles activities and access. Moser reviews planning. The Social Relations Approach analyses institutions and power. The matrix works with communities. **Frameworks are aids to thinking**, so adapt their categories to your setting.
notes.91: Fill this profile with women and men separately and compare. The dairy example shows a programme that would raise milk yields while income and decisions stay with men. The design response is concrete: enrol women as members and pay into their accounts. **Disagreements between versions are findings.**
notes.92: Use the checklist at design, mid-term and before scale-up. Each item points to a section, so a 'no' tells you where to read. The last sentence is a safeguard: **a checklist is a prompt for discussion with women** in the programme area and does not replace it.
notes.93: Pick indicators that cover all three of Kabeer's dimensions plus norms. Report each for women and men at baseline and endline. Using NFHS wording **lets you compare your area with the district or state**, which saves you inventing a benchmark.
notes.94: Follow the table row by row to see how the tools turn into design changes: the activity profile, time use, bargaining, intersection and risk. The goat programme in Bihar is illustrative. The conclusion is the target: **meet a practical need in a way that builds strategic gains**.
notes.95: Place your programme on the four-step scale: gender-blind, aware, responsive, relation-changing. Most sit in the middle. Be accurate in proposals, since claiming transformation for a change in meeting times costs credibility. **Ask which relation changed, for whom, and what evidence shows it.**
notes.97: Treat the six mistakes as a pre-review checklist. Each has a cause and a correction. The one that costs most is assuming household pooling, so decide and record whose name is on the benefit. **Return to the relevant section** when a review raises a mistake.
notes.98: Read the ten ideas as a summary of the course. The numbers behind them have sources you can open. The second column holds the evidence: missing girls, undercounted work, 289 minutes a day of unpaid domestic work for women aged 6 and over in 2024, rare help-seeking, slow policy change. **Check the latest round** before quoting a figure.
notes.99: Choose the next course by your work. Gender Mainstreaming covers budgeting and institutions, Women's Economic Empowerment covers livelihoods and credit, and Care Economy covers unpaid care. The suggested order is stated at the bottom. **Start with Mainstreaming**, then pick one depending on your work.
